newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-LLOYD GIVES DAMNING POST-MORTEM ON WEST INDIES.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-LLOYD GIVES DAMNING POST-MORTEM ON WEST INDIES.

text.p: West Indies team manager Clive Lloyd criticised star batsman Brian Lara and selectors on Thursday after declaring the once mighty cricket power faced a difficult future.

Lloyd, who captained West Indies at the height of their prowess during the late 1970s and early 1980s, spoke out in frustration two days after the tourists slumped to their heaviest test loss in 40 years.
Australia beat West Indies by an innings and 183 runs on Tuesday in the fourth test at Adelaide Oval to clinch the five-test series 3-1 and retain the Frank Worrell trophy with one match to spare.

Lloyd said vice-captain Lara must apply himself more and temper his attacking instincts after failing to score a half-century in the series until the second innings in Adelaide, when the match was all but lost.

"Brian's one of those batsmen who likes to score quickly but he's got to realise in test cricket he's got to work harder," Lloyd told reporters as the tourists prepared for the fifth test, starting at Perth's WACA Ground on Saturday.
"Bowlers have studied him and worked out how to restrict his scoring," he said.
In the second and third tests, Lara, the world record holder for the highest score in test and first class cricket, scored seven runs in four innings.
Lloyd said the squad sent to Australia lacked balance with the absence of a frontline spinner and an all-rounder.

In a frank assessment of West Indies' current weaknesses, Lloyd said: "We still haven't got a good opening pair yet, our middle order is still there or thereabouts and our back-up bowlers haven't been too good."

"We have to have a look and choose carefully (in selecting future teams) because they (the players) are quite young. It's not a rosy future as such but once we get the right blend we're going to be a very competitive team in the next year or so.
"We should have brought an all-rounder, somebody like Phil Simmons who had been here before, a seasoned player, full of confidence.
"It would have helped us a lot because we wouldn't have had to put so much pressure on our older bowlers," said Lloyd, referring to ageing pace duo Curtly Ambrose and captain Courtney Walsh.
Simmons arrived in Australia two weeks ago after fast bowlers Kenneth Benjamin and Nixon McLean went home injured.
"A spinner who is good enough should have been here and would have got enough experience looking at (Australia leg-spinner) Shane Warne and the others."
West Indies next play India in a five-test series in the Caribbean starting next month.
West Indies built their success over the past two decades on a four-pronged pace attack that battered opponents into submission.
The tactic, described as obsolete by Australia captain Mark Taylor, failed dismally in the current test series.

"There comes a time when you have to look at a situation and think, 'Are we going to have competitive fast bowlers that are able to win games for you?' and if they don't then you've got to think again," Lloyd said.
